title: Jeremiah 33:1–13
context: Jeremiah 33:1–13 records the LORD’s word to Jeremiah a second time while he is still confined in the court of the guard. The LORD, the maker who establishes what he forms, invites him: "Call to me, and I will answer you." The question of how prayer relates to what God does is discussed at Joshua 10:14, and this verse does not reopen it. The houses of Jerusalem, even the royal houses, have been torn down to strengthen the defenses, and the city is filling with the dead. Yet the LORD promises health, healing, peace, and truth, restored fortunes for Judah and Israel, cleansing and pardon for all their iniquity, and a city that will bring him a name of joy before the nations. In a land now called waste, the voices of bride and bridegroom will be heard again, with worshipers saying, "Give thanks to the LORD of Armies, for the LORD is good, for his loving kindness endures forever" (compare Psalm 136:1), and shepherds will again count their flocks in every region.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah the second time, while he was still locked up in the court of the guard, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Jeremiah a second time while he is still confined in the court of the guard. Arminian readers see God continuing to speak to his servant even when his circumstances have not changed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s word as not bound by human restrictions. Both traditions read the verse as linking this chapter closely with chapter 32, both set during Jeremiah’s confinement.

verses.text: “The LORD who does it, the LORD who forms it to establish it—the LORD is his name, says:
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD who does it and forms it to establish it, whose name is the LORD, speaks. Arminians see God introducing himself as the one who carries out his purposes, which gives weight to what follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God as the one who plans and accomplishes his will. Both traditions note that the object of it is not stated, and many read it as God’s purpose or his creation; they hold the question open.

verses.text: ‘Call to me, and I will answer you, and will show you great and difficult things, which you don’t know.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah to call to him, and he will answer and show him great and difficult things he does not know. Arminian readers see God’s invitation to prayer, which shows that he wants his people to seek him and receive his revelation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God graciously revealing his purposes. Both traditions hold this invitation as shared ground, and they note that how prayer relates to what God does is discussed at Joshua 10:14.

verses.text: For the LORD, the God of Israel, says concerning the houses of this city and concerning the houses of the kings of Judah, which are broken down to make a defense against the mounds and against the sword:
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks about the houses of Jerusalem and the royal houses torn down to strengthen defenses against the siege mounds and sword. Arminians see the desperate situation of the city, which the coming promises will reverse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the destruction as the background for God’s word of hope. Both traditions read the detail as reflecting the reality of the siege, when buildings were sacrificed for the city’s defense.

verses.text: ‘While men come to fight with the Chaldeans, and to fill them with the dead bodies of men, whom I have killed in my anger and in my wrath, and for all whose wickedness I have hidden my face from this city,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the houses will be filled with the dead whom he has struck in his anger, because he has hidden his face from the city for its wickedness. Arminian readers see the seriousness of judgment, which follows the city’s persistent sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s hidden face as a sign of judgment. Both traditions read the verse soberly, as part of the contrast between present disaster and the healing promised in the next verse.

verses.text: behold, I will bring it health and healing, and I will cure them; and I will reveal to them abundance of peace and truth.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will bring health and healing, cure them, and reveal abundance of peace and truth. Arminians see God’s mercy going beyond judgment to bring complete restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s healing as a gift of grace. Both traditions note the contrast with the false prophets’ empty promises of peace in 6:14, since this peace comes with truth.

verses.text: I will restore the fortunes of Judah and Israel, and will build them as at the first.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will restore the fortunes of Judah and Israel and build them as at the first. Arminian readers see the restoration of both kingdoms, which points to a renewed and united people of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s covenant faithfulness in restoring both houses. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and note that the hope of a reunited people appears throughout the prophets (compare Ezekiel 37:15–22).

verses.text: I will cleanse them from all their iniquity by which they have sinned against me. I will pardon all their iniquities by which they have sinned against me and by which they have transgressed against me.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will cleanse them from all their iniquity and pardon all their sins and transgressions. Arminians see God’s forgiveness as the foundation of restoration, freely offered to his repentant people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s grace in pardoning sin. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and connect it with the new covenant promise that God will remember sin no more (31:34).

verses.text: This city will be to me for a name of joy, for praise, and for glory, before all the nations of the earth, which will hear all the good that I do to them, and will fear and tremble for all the good and for all the peace that I provide to it.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the city will be a name of joy, praise, and glory before all nations, who will fear and tremble at the good he does. Arminian readers see God’s blessing on his people as a witness to the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s glory displayed through his work of restoration. Both traditions note that the nations’ fear and trembling here comes from seeing God’s goodness, not his judgment.

verses.text: The LORD says: “Yet again there will be heard in this place, about which you say, ‘It is waste, without man and without animal, even in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem, that are desolate, without man and without inhabitant and without animal,’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that in the place the people call a waste without people or animals, there will again be heard sounds of life. Arminians see God answering the people’s despair with a promise of renewal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God reversing what seemed final. Both traditions note that the verse takes up the people’s description of desolation, just as 32:43 did, in order to answer it.

verses.text: the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the voice of those who say, ‘Give thanks to the LORD of Armies, for the LORD is good, for his loving kindness endures forever;’ who bring thanksgiving into the LORD’s house. For I will cause the captivity of the land to be reversed as at the first,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the voices of joy, bride and bridegroom, and worshipers saying "Give thanks to the LORD of Armies, for the LORD is good, for his loving kindness endures forever" will return. Arminian readers see the reversal of earlier judgments (compare 7:34 and 16:9), where these voices were silenced.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the restoration of joy and worship. Both traditions note the echo of Psalm 136:1, "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good," and they read the verse as showing that restored worship is central to God’s promise.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says: “Yet again there will be in this place, which is waste, without man and without animal, and in all its cities, a habitation of shepherds causing their flocks to lie down.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says there will again be pasture for shepherds and their flocks in this waste place and all its cities. Arminians see the return of peaceful, ordinary life, which shows the completeness of God’s restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image of shepherds as a picture of peace and provision. Both traditions read the verse as part of the promise that the land will again be inhabited and productive.

verses.text: In the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the lowland, in the cities of the South, in the land of Benjamin, in the places around Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, the flocks will again pass under the hands of him who counts them,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says flocks will again pass under the hands of the one who counts them in all the regions of Judah and Benjamin. Arminian readers see a detailed picture of restored life, extending to every part of the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the counting of flocks as a sign of order and care. Both traditions note that the list of regions matches 32:44, tying the two chapters together, and some read the one who counts as a hint of the shepherd-king who follows.
